note.text: A motorway is designed for controlled access and through movement, with connections concentrated at junctions. Its usefulness depends on demand and links to other roads; it does not provide a doorway to every settlement. A cableway moves supported cabins or loads along a cable route between terminals. It may cross difficult terrain but has capacity, weather, maintenance and safety constraints.

sections.heading: Your goal and connections
sections.text: By the end, you should be able to match specialised infrastructure to a stated need and limitation. Builds on: transport modes and route constraints. Leads to: pipeline networks.

sections.heading: Follow the local example or model
sections.text: An invented corridor has heavy through traffic and a proposal for controlled-access movement. A separate steep-slope site considers a cableway between fixed terminals. These proposals solve different movement problems. Neither model authorises local construction or states that a particular Cameroonian project is operating.

sections.heading: Apply and check
sections.text: Identify traffic type, terrain and access need. Explain why a specialised system may help, then state a limitation and the connecting service needed. Do not assume a motorway junction or cable terminal serves every doorstep.

pick.q: An invented motorway bypass has no junction beside a village. What should a planner investigate?
pick.r: The village’s feeder connection to an authorised junction
w: Assume every home has direct entry
Replace all local roads with no connections
Ignore the village’s access needs
e: Controlled access limits direct entry.
Local journeys still need connections.
A bypass can change access for nearby people.
pick.y: Assess through movement and local access separately.

pick.q: A fictional cableway links fixed hillside terminals. What is a relevant limitation?
pick.r: Loads must reach and leave those terminals
w: Every nearby doorstep is automatically served
No maintenance can be needed
Cableways have unlimited capacity
e: Fixed terminals constrain access.
Cables and equipment need maintenance.
Equipment and operating conditions limit capacity.
pick.y: A terrain advantage does not remove terminal constraints.

pick.q: A proposed specialised route has little demand and high maintenance needs. What follows?
pick.r: Its suitability needs a cost and demand assessment
w: Its specialised name proves it is worthwhile
Every community must build one
Terrain and demand no longer matter
e: A name is not performance evidence.
Systems should match needs and resources.
Terrain and demand remain relevant.
pick.y: Explain conditions rather than promising universal benefit.
